[RESPONSE] I’ve been dealing with severe itching in my vulvar area for about a year, and I’ve also had increasing pain during sex over that same time — it’s gotten so bad that we’ve mostly stopped being intimate recently.

[THOUGHT] The patient presents with chronic (1-year) vulvar pruritus and dyspareunia — two hallmark symptoms of vulvar dermatoses, particularly lichen sclerosus or lichen planus. These conditions are common causes of chronic vulvar symptoms and can lead to scarring, architectural changes, and significant functional impairment. Key differentiating features include skin appearance (e.g., porcelain-white plaques, purpura, erosions), presence of fissures or scarring, and associated systemic symptoms. Since visual inspection is essential for diagnosis — especially to assess for classic signs like ivory-white plaques, loss of architecture, or mucosal involvement — the next critical step is a focused physical examination.

[TEST] Vulvar examination (with good lighting and gentle retraction, noting color, texture, integrity, architecture, presence of fissures, excoriations, or sclerosis).

5. External Genitalia: Dry, thin, white plaque-like lesions on the vulva.  
6. External Genitalia: Atrophy of the labia minora.  
7. External Genitalia: Retraction of the clitoris.  
8. External Genitalia: Pale and wrinkled perianal skin.

[THOUGHT] The physical findings — ivory-white plaques, vulvar atrophy, labial minora resorption, clitoral hood retraction, and perianal involvement with pale, wrinkled skin — are highly characteristic of lichen sclerosus. This chronic inflammatory dermatosis predominantly affects postmenopausal women but can occur at any age. It carries a small but well-documented risk of squamous cell carcinoma, especially with long-standing, untreated disease. While biopsy is the gold standard for confirmation (particularly to rule out malignancy or overlapping conditions like lichen planus), the clinical presentation here is classic and strongly suggestive. However, given the diagnostic importance of histopathology in guiding management and surveillance — and because biopsy is minimally invasive and definitive — it remains the most appropriate next step to confirm diagnosis and exclude dysplasia or early malignancy.

[TEST] Punch biopsy of an active white plaque on the vulva (preferably from a symptomatic or atypical area, avoiding ulcerated or scarred regions).
14. Biopsy of vulvar lesions histopathology: Hyperkeratosis with a thinning of the epidermis and loss of rete ridges, sclerotic changes in the dermis.

[THOUGHT] The histopathology report shows hyperkeratosis, epidermal thinning (atrophy), loss of rete ridges, and dermal sclerosis — the classic triad of lichen sclerosus. These findings, combined with the highly characteristic clinical features (ivory-white plaques, labial atrophy, clitoral retraction, perianal involvement), confirm the diagnosis with high specificity. No other common vulvar dermatosis (e.g., lichen planus, psoriasis, candidiasis) matches this exact constellation of clinical and histologic features. Given the strength and consistency of the evidence across history, exam, and biopsy, further testing is unnecessary and would delay definitive management.

[DIAGNOSIS] Lichen sclerosus
